title: Three Pictures of Feature Geometry
takeaway: A hand-drawn contrast between three ways features might be arranged in activation space: evenly spread one-dimensional directions, clumped one-dimensional directions, and continuous higher-dimensional patches. The last panel is the one that bites: if a model uses feature manifolds rather than rays, dictionary learning can only ever approximate them with discrete directions, and asking for the "correct number of features" stops being a well-posed question.
walkthrough:
Three grey circles sit side by side. Each is a cartoon of the activation space the [[sparse-autoencoder]] decomposes — the 512-dimensional space of MLP neuron activations, squashed onto the page. A dot inside a circle is one [[feature]] direction. The boundary carries no meaning; it just fences in the drawing. Nothing here is measured. The panels are three competing pictures of how features held in [[superposition]] sit relative to each other.

**Left: "isotropic superposition."** The dots are scattered roughly evenly. This is the picture inherited from [[toy-models-of-superposition]], and the caption says features "repel and spread as far apart as possible" because overlap costs [[interference]]. Discrete and one-dimensional is the key assumption here. One-dimensional means a feature's entire range is a single ray: a fixed unit direction $d$, and a scalar activation $a \ge 0$ contributing $a\,d$. That scalar carries intensity or confidence and nothing else.

**Middle: "anisotropic superposition."** Same dots, but several are gathered into tight clumps. The paper says its own results push it toward this picture, since related features come out with small angles between their dictionary vectors. It offers two reasons: the features fire together ([[correlated-features]]), or they push up the same next tokens ([[action-sharing-features]]). It suspects the second matters more.

Neither of these two panels threatens completeness. Features are still rays, so one dictionary entry per ray finishes the job; the entries are just spread unevenly in the middle case.

**Right: "feature manifolds."** Beside the loose dots are three shaded shapes — a crescent, a wedge, an ellipse. Each stands for a continuous, higher-dimensional patch of directions the model actually uses, rather than a single ray. [[dictionary-learning]] can only place discrete vectors, so it would cover a patch by sprinkling rays across it.

That is the consequence the panel is built to deliver. If some manifolds admit no unique description in terms of finitely many one-dimensional features, extra dictionary entries keep buying finer resolution and never terminate — so the [[correct-number-of-features]] is not well posed, and the [[feature-splitting]] already observed may be that approximation in progress. The paper puts this forward as a hypothesis, not a finding, and notes it is not exclusive of the other two.

terms.definition: The bounding outline of each panel, standing in for the whole activation space in which feature directions live — here the 512-dimensional space of MLP neuron activations. The circular shape is drawing convention; only the arrangement of things inside it is meant to carry information.

One feature direction: a single unit vector in activation space, drawn as a point. A dot represents a feature whose activations lie along one ray, so the only thing that varies is how strongly it fires.

A feature whose whole set of possible contributions is a ray — a fixed direction scaled by a non-negative activation. The activation encodes only intensity, so the feature has no way to express which of several related things is present.

What the scalar activation of a one-dimensional feature is taken to mean: how strongly, or with how much confidence, the feature's property is present. The paper elsewhere says its features do look like this, which it counts as evidence for superposition.

The name the paper gives, retrospectively, to the picture it inherited from its earlier toy-models work: discrete one-dimensional features that repel each other into a roughly evenly spaced arrangement. Isotropic means the arrangement looks statistically the same in every direction.

The hypothesis that a network represents more independent features than it has neurons, by assigning each feature its own direction in activation space rather than its own neuron. All three panels are pictures of how those directions might be laid out.
The behavior that produces the left panel's even spread: because non-orthogonal directions cross-talk, the training pressure pushes feature directions apart from each other.
The authors' own earlier work, Toy Models of Superposition, which produced the isotropic picture from small synthetic models. This figure is the paper revising that inheritance.

The tight groups of dots in the middle panel: sets of features whose directions sit at small angles to each other rather than spreading out. The paper reports seeing this in its actual dictionaries, via UMAP projections of the learned directions.

The middle panel's picture: features are still one-dimensional, but their directions are distributed unevenly, dense in some regions and sparse elsewhere. Anisotropic means the arrangement is not the same in every direction.

The right panel's shaded shapes: continuous, higher-dimensional sets of directions that the model might use as a single unit, instead of one isolated ray. The paper raises this as a possibility it cannot rule out, not as something it has demonstrated.

Three drawn manifolds, differing in shape only to suggest that such patches need not be simple or convex. A curved crescent, in particular, is a patch that no finite set of rays can describe uniquely.

The claim that when the true object is a continuous patch, the learned dictionary does not recover it — it lays discrete directions across it and returns those. The learned features are then artifacts of resolution rather than the model's real units.

Writing each activation vector as a sparse weighted sum of directions drawn from a fixed, over-large set. The set is discrete by construction, which is exactly why a continuous manifold is a problem for it.

The paper's observation that widening the autoencoder turns one feature into several more specific ones covering the same territory. The right panel offers a possible cause: the extra features are finer samples of a manifold.
Features that tend to be active at the same time — one of the two explanations the paper offers for why directions clump in the middle panel.

Features that push up roughly the same next-token predictions and therefore need to produce similar neuron activations, ending up at similar directions. The paper suspects this, rather than correlated firing, is the main cause of clumping.
The dictionary size at which every feature the model uses has been recovered and no more. Under the manifold hypothesis this quantity may not exist.

numbers.meaning: The number of panels, and so the number of competing hypotheses drawn: isotropic superposition, anisotropic superposition, and feature manifolds. The paper states these are not mutually exclusive, so three panels are three ingredients rather than three alternatives you must choose between.
The dimensionality of a feature under the first two panels. A one-dimensional feature is a ray: direction fixed, one scalar free. This is the assumption the third panel drops.

The dimensionality of a feature manifold in the right panel. The shapes are drawn as 2-D patches only because the page is 2-D; the hypothesis is just that the dimensionality exceeds one, and the paper names no specific value because it has not measured one.

The number of loose feature directions drawn in each panel. This is illustrative crowding, chosen so the eye can compare spacing across panels — it stands for nothing measured, since a real dictionary here holds thousands of directions.
The size and count of the tight groups. Again illustrative: the paper reports clusters of related features in its UMAP projections but does not attach these counts to any of them.
Three manifolds drawn alongside the loose dots, indicating the hypothesis is that some features are manifolds and others remain ordinary rays — not that every feature becomes a patch.

The dimension of the space each circle abstracts: the one-layer transformer under study has a 512-neuron ReLU MLP, and each learned feature is a 512-dimensional column of the decoder matrix $W_d$. The circle is that space flattened to two dimensions for drawing.

The dictionary sizes of the paper's three main autoencoder runs (A/0, A/1, A/2). They matter to this figure because it is the increase across these sizes that produces feature splitting — the phenomenon the right panel proposes to reinterpret as ever-finer sampling of a manifold, with no size at which sampling would be complete.
